items.title: Emile Barnes Interview, 1960-07-29
items.q: You know that time you cut the records with Charlie Love?

ctx.x: Well, I'll tell you how George was. He was a, to me he was a sweet clarinet player. You know, he just took his time and made that. You know, he didn't rough it out. But he had that one way. Now for a band man, he wasn't that much, he ain't a band man. But he was a tough man in the parade. And you could hear him way down there but so sweet. Now your man, your good band man, real band man, that was Louis, which we called Big Eye Louis. In the orchestra you mean? Yeah. In the orchestra. That's really, Charlie can…

You know that time you cut the records with Charlie Love? Do you remember that? Was it on St. Louis Street near Decatur? That's right, yeah. Uh huh. Well it seemed to me as the evening went on, you changed your whole tone and style and everything, you know? Yeah. You played different. You played different that night from any other time I heard you. I don't think they issued the stuff, you know, late in the evening where you began to play very different.
Uh huh. Well I, I don't know. I played different always.

items.title: Emile Barnes Interview, 1962-01-03
items.q: Did he play anything like Charlie Love? No.

ctx.x: No. Now was he the leader of the band? Yeah. This Edwauke Clem? Yeah. He was the leader of the band. What kind of style did he play? Can you think of anybody that we heard that he played like? Let's see who. I don't remember now. Well like Kid Thomas?

Well partly like Thomas. Yeah partly like Thomas. How about Charlie Love? But he had a, a, a tongue in his thing. You know like cutting over. Uh huh. See a, see a cutting over the tongue like that. Did he play anything like Charlie Love? No. I think it's more like Thomas.
Did he have any feature number?
